title: Two-way radio (walkie-talkie): safe teardown
summary: A working two-way radio is worth far more whole: keep it with its pack, antenna and charger. A dead one gives a battery pack (7.2–7.4 V on the Baofeng and Kenwood models checked), a desk charger, a matched antenna, a speaker and an antenna socket. Check the lithium pack for swelling before you charge or open anything, and never transmit without the antenna on.

steps.text: Check the battery before you charge or open anything. Read the pack label first: it names the chemistry (Li-ion, Ni-MH or Ni-Cd). Switch the radio off, press the pack's release latch and slide the pack off. Look and feel for swelling, a split case, heat or a sweet smell. A lithium pack with any of these goes straight to safety_swollen_lithium. AA or AAA cells with white crust have leaked: take them out wearing gloves and safety glasses, and keep your hands off your face. A NiMH or NiCd pack that is split, crusty or wet with liquid has leaked too: tape its contacts, set it on stone and don't charge it.
steps.warn: Never charge, use or open a swollen, hot or damaged pack. Leaked NiMH or NiCd electrolyte is a corrosive alkali that burns: keep it off skin and out of eyes. If it gets on you, rinse with lots of clean water for 15 minutes; eyes need medical help.

steps.text: Test it whole. Screw the antenna on by its base. Never charge a wet pack: wipe it dry with a cloth, no heat. Measure a lithium pack first: a two-cell pack that reads under about 4 V has sat flat, so put it in the reject box and don't charge it (test_lithium_cell). Then charge the pack in the radio's own desk charger, on stone or a metal tray, where you can watch it, and unplug it if the pack gets warm. In sets that take AA or AAA cells, charge only cells marked rechargeable, in a charger approved for that radio, and never charge alkaline cells: they can leak or burst (Energizer non-rechargeable FAQ). Switch on and listen; with two radios on one channel, check they hear each other. Channels and licences: reference_radio_signals.
steps.warn: Never transmit without the antenna fitted: a poor match can damage the final transistors. Don't use a radio with a damaged antenna (it can burn skin) or hold the antenna while you talk. Keep radios off, and don't charge them, near fuel vapour or gas: a spark can ignite it.

steps.text: If it works, stop here. A working radio is worth far more whole than in parts. Keep it with its pack, antenna, charger and any speaker-mic or earpiece.

To open a dead one: radio off and pack off. Put tape over the pack's contacts, keep keys, coins and jewellery away from them, and store the pack on a non-flammable surface. Don't open the pack itself.
steps.warn: Battery makers say never to take a pack apart. Lithium packs hold cells wired together with a protection board (the Kenwood KNB-55L is two cells in series), and a slip shorts them.

steps.text: Unscrew the antenna by its base, not its tip. Pull the volume and channel knobs straight off, or use a knob remover if your radio needs one (Motorola lists one for the CP200). Don't force them. Undo any round nuts under the knobs and round the antenna socket, if your radio has them, with a nut driver or pliers.

Find the case screws: look on the back, by the battery rails, under the belt clip and under labels. Some radios use small Torx screws (T6 on the Motorola CP200). Take them all out and keep them in a jar.
Lift the metal chassis out of the front case. If it sticks, ease the case apart with a plastic tool or old card, working round the seam. Go slowly: the speaker and microphone are wired to the board.
Unsolder or cut the speaker and microphone wires close to the board, then lift the speaker out of its holder. Keep the wires on the speaker as long as you can.
Free the board only if you want parts from it. Unplug any flat flex cable first, then undo the screws that hold the board to the chassis (13 on the Kenwood TK-3360). Lift it out by its edges.
steps.warn: Static can kill the chips. Touch bare metal on the chassis before you handle the board, and hold it by its edges.

steps.text: Take the antenna socket (SMA or BNC) with its nut and bracket, and the earphone and microphone jacks. Unsolder them or cut them out with a short tail of board.

Leave desk chargers and their wall adapters whole. Plug in only an adapter with an uncracked case and an undamaged cord. Test a charger with a pack you know is good, on stone or a metal tray, watched: the light should change as the pack charges. Don't open the mains adapter; if you must, follow teardown_phone_charger.
steps.warn: Charge only the pack type the charger was made for, and unplug it if the pack gets warm.

steps.text: Store packs cool and dry in a metal tin, away from where people sleep, with tape over the contacts. Baofeng says to charge a pack before storing it and to recharge stored lithium packs about every 6 months.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **The whole radio, working.** Talking between groups with no network. Height matters more than anything else for range (build_yagi_antenna). Radios from one charging rack may be set up alike: try them together. Channels, emergency calls and licences: reference_radio_signals.
- **Battery packs.** The packs for the Baofeng and Kenwood radios here are 7.2–7.4 V. The Kenwood TK-3360's KNB-55L is a 7.4 V Li-ion pack of two 3.7 V cells, 1480 mAh, with a protection circuit; its KNB-56N is a 7.2 V NiMH pack of six 1.2 V cells, 1400 mAh (Kenwood TK-3360). The Motorola CP200 runs on 7.5 V ±20% and takes 2250 mAh or 1600 mAh Li-ion, 1400 mAh NiMH or 950 mAh NiCd packs (CP200 spec sheet). The Baofeng UV-5R uses a 7.4 V 1800 mAh Li-ion pack (UV-5R manual). Use a pack with the radio family it was made for: CP200 packs carry a resistor that tells the radio which chemistry is inside (CP200 service manual).
- **Desk chargers.** Use a charger only with the pack type it was made for. The UV-5R's desk charger takes the radio or the pack alone, runs from a plug-in adapter and shows red while charging and green when full (UV-5R manual).
- **Antenna.** A rubber-duck antenna matched to the radio's band. The UV-5R has a male SMA socket and its antenna a female SMA plug (Lidberg UV-5R). Keep each antenna with its radio.
- **Speaker.** A small speaker for alarms, intercoms and radio repairs. The CP200 drives a 24 Ω internal speaker with 500 mW (CP200 service manual); the TK-3360 is rated 500 mW at 8 Ω (Kenwood TK-3360). Test: touch it to a 1.5 V cell and it clicks.
- **Speaker-mics and earpieces.** Keep them with radios that fit them.
- **The board.** Honestly, little. It holds fine surface-mount parts: an RF power module, crystals, 5 V and 3 V regulators and a 3 A fuse on the battery feed in the CP200 (CP200 service manual). Take the antenna socket and jacks; leave the rest unless you repair radios.

## Radio and battery safety

- Never transmit without an antenna (Lidberg UV-5R).
- Don't use a radio with a damaged antenna: it can give a minor burn. Don't hold the antenna while transmitting, keep the radio and antenna at least 2.5 cm (1 in) from your face, and transmit no more than half the time (Motorola RF safety).
- Don't take battery packs apart, crush or puncture them, or dry a wet one with heat; keep jewellery, keys and chains off the contacts; don't burn them (Motorola RF safety).
- Baofeng says to charge packs between 5 and 40 °C, never to charge a wet pack, and never to take one apart (UV-5R manual).
- NiMH cells hold an alkaline electrolyte that is corrosive and can cause chemical burns, and gas vented from a cell can carry it out to form crystals or rust (Energizer NiMH). NiCd cells hold a potassium hydroxide electrolyte that can burn skin and eyes (Tenergy NiCd SDS). For a leaking cell wear gloves and safety glasses. If electrolyte gets on skin, wash it off with plenty of water at once; for eyes, rinse for 15 minutes and get medical help (Tenergy NiCd SDS).
- Some business radios are certified intrinsically safe for explosive atmospheres. Motorola says repairs to its intrinsically safe radios must be done at a site audited under the certifier's standard, and that only a radio certified for hazardous locations may be carried into a potentially explosive atmosphere (Motorola RF safety). Don't assume a radio you have opened still meets its certification.
- Turn the radio off, and don't charge it or swap packs or antennas, anywhere there may be fuel vapour, gas or other explosive material: a spark can start a fire or explosion (UV-5R manual; Motorola RF safety).
- Don't modify the radio (UV-5R manual).

## Variations

- **Baofeng UV-5R:** dual-band ham handheld. The pack slides off its rails when you press the release (Lidberg UV-5R). A full teardown needs a screw hidden under the display (hamskey UV-5R).
- **Kenwood TK-3360:** UHF business radio, 450–520 MHz, 5 W. Take off the volume and selector knobs and two screws, and the chassis lifts out of the case; the speaker and microphone wires are soldered to the board, and 13 screws hold it to the chassis (Kenwood TK-3360).
- **Motorola CP200:** UHF version 438–470 MHz. Its chassis screws are T6 Torx, Motorola lists a knob remover and chassis opener tool for the front cover, and it uses an anti-static kit for all work inside (CP200 service manual).
- **NiCd packs** are listed for the CP200 (950 mAh, CP200 spec sheet). NiCd cells hold toxic cadmium: keep the pack whole and never burn or crush it.
- **Consumer radios** may take AA or AAA cells or a small NiMH pack; check the label in the battery space.

## What to leave

- The insides of battery packs.
- Surface-mount chips and the RF power module, unless you repair radios.
- Cracked antennas.

## Testing what you got out

- **Radio:** power it and listen on a busy channel; with two radios, check they hear each other at range.
- **NiMH cells:** a charged cell reads about 1.4 V with no load and sits near 1.2 V in use (Energizer NiMH).
- **Lithium packs:** measure the pack, then see test_lithium_cell. Two cells in series read about twice one cell, so a two-cell pack under about 4 V has a cell below 2 V: don't charge it.
- **Antenna:** the only sure test is on a working radio, talking to another one.
